$comment: Central config for the /rca-build RCA harness. Product and infra values live here rather than in code. The `capabilities` block DESCRIBES capabilities and never instructs: no probe commands, because a command string arriving as data with customer scope interpolated in required a whole execution gate and produced an injection escape anyway. Vendor names appear ONLY as `seedHints` — non-authoritative hints for the common cases, which an agent assignment always overrides. That distinction is the point: a hint list can never know the customer's stack, and one that pretended to told New Relic users to install promtool. No reportFile: the plugin never writes a local RCA report — the full report lives on the Test Observability UI (triggerRcaReport).
$concurrencyComment: Max coordinator subagents run in parallel during Step 5 fan-out. HONORED LITERALLY on the default path (direct Agent-tool dispatch of ai-tfa-coordinator subagents — one message, up to `concurrency` tool-use blocks per batch). Only a SOFT target on the opt-in Workflow-tool path (workflows/rca-batch.mjs), which the Workflow runtime hard-caps at min(16, cpu cores - 2) regardless of this value — that cap is architectural and cannot be raised from this repo. See SKILL.md Step 5.
$softPendingDrainComment: tfaRcaTurn abandons its in-call poll at pollSoftPendingMs (90s) and returns a soft PENDING while the TFA agent keeps working — turns finalizing past 90s are routine. On a soft PENDING the loop READS the same turnId via getTfaTurnResult on this budget before it routes asks or submits anything further; reads do not consume turnCap. Only when the budget is spent does the run end PENDING (pending-resume row).
$maxErrorReadsComment: A soft PENDING is drained on the full budget below, but a HARD read failure (a thrown error, or a result whose status/message says the TFA agent run failed) is a different signal: it will not resolve by asking again. After this many CONSECUTIVE failed reads the drain stops early and the row ends PENDING with a `tfa-error` note, still resumable. A single good read clears the streak. Measured motivation: on one real build, drain reads plus their sleeps were 23% of all coordinator tool calls, and the four tests that wedged this way were the four slowest in the batch.

paths.$comment: State CSV path is ALWAYS derived per build via lib/csv-state.mjs csvPathFor(buildId, stateDir): the build id is in the filename (no cross-build collisions) and the default directory is OS temp (<tmpdir>/bstack-rca/), so the harness never pollutes the invoking workspace. Set stateDir only to retain the CSV somewhere specific (e.g. a CI artifact dir).

evidenceRouting.$comment: Inbound evidenceType -> capability. The KEYS are the TFA agent's wire vocabulary, not ours: `k8s` and `kibana` arrive as those literals and route to the generic `infra` and `logs` capabilities, which is exactly the indirection this map exists for. Several evidenceTypes share one capability (product_code, deploy and ci all route to github), which is why the capability table is a sibling block rather than rows in here.

$capabilitiesComment: The capability table. Keyed by CAPABILITY, joined to evidenceRouting by name — a sibling block, not rows inside evidenceRouting, because buildManifest enumerates Object.values(evidenceRouting) and a capability-keyed row placed there becomes a phantom manifest entry. Rows DESCRIBE, they do not instruct. There are no probe commands here: a command string arriving as data with a customer value interpolated into it required a command-execution gate, an interpolation guard and a per-executable probe table, and produced a shell-injection escape, an attached-flag bypass and a write-tool dispatch on the MCP route regardless. It was also never generic — a fingerprint list only knows the vendors someone wrote down, so a New Relic customer matched nothing and was told to install promtool. `intent` is what the agent reasons from instead; `seedHints` are hints for the common cases and are NEVER authoritative — an agent assignment always wins.
$probeComment: Probes are validated by isProbeRunnable() in lib/tool-cache.mjs, NOT by isRunnable(). isRunnable exists to judge cacheability: it allows pipelines into ALLOWED_FILTER (which includes python3, awk, sed) and restricts leaders to gh/kubectl/curl/git — so it both permits `curl X | python3` and refuses `docker ps`. Probe rules instead: one command, no pipeline, no operators, no redirects, no mutation, and a leader present in BOTH the global catalog and this row's own fingerprint executables. Placeholders are brace-form {field}; an unquoted < is read as a file redirect and rejected.

github.intent: Read the product's code and its merged-PR history. Verified means: a specific repository is readable AND the base branch's merged-PR list can be listed, because the culprit-PR hunt is the run's entire output. Reached through a git-forge CLI or an MCP server for one — whichever this machine has.

repos.consumer: PR-window search and path-overlap falsification (Step 4; references/code-evidence.md)

subpaths.consumer: path-overlap falsification inside a monorepo (Step 4; references/code-evidence.md)

baseBranch.consumer: the merged-PR window the Step 4 culprit hunt searches

infra.intent: Reach the runtime the service under test actually runs on — a container orchestrator, a scheduler, a serverless platform, a process manager, a plain VM. There is no default: identify what THIS team uses. Verified means the runtime answers for the specific scope named below, not merely that some runtime CLI exists on PATH.

runtimeKind.consumer: recorded as the manifest's `via`, so a coordinator knows which runtime it is talking to

namespace.consumer: the scope Step 4's per-workload sweeps target

workloads.consumer: maps a failure signature to the workload whose logs Step 4 sweeps

logs.intent: Query the application's own logs — NOT test logs, which TFA owns and this run never gathers. Any log store: hosted, self-run, or a CLI against one. Verified means a query against the named index or stream returns, so a Step 4 sweep will find something to read.

logIndex.consumer: the index or stream Step 4's per-workload log sweep queries

serviceNames.consumer: maps a failure signature to the service whose logs to sweep in Step 4

metrics.intent: Read resource and saturation signals — memory, CPU, error rate, latency — so a failure that looks functional can be recognised as pressure instead. Any metrics backend. Verified means a query returns for the named scope.

metricsNamespace.consumer: scopes the memory/CPU pressure lookup Step 4 runs alongside the log sweep

other.$comment: The catch-all for a stack nothing else classifies. By definition it has nothing to recognise, so it declares no seedHints and no intent — permitted because resolvable is always-asked. exemptFromDiscoveryReport keeps it out of the human-facing 'not available' line, where it would appear every single run; the manifest and the TFA-facing declaration still mark it unavailable.
